item.title: How to Escape the Grips of a Manipulative Partner
item.description:
Relationships

How to Escape the Grips of a Manipulative Partner

Manipulation comes under the microscope in new relationship research.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • The contributors to manipulativeness in a relationship range from psychopathy to emotional dominance.
  • A new study teases apart the contributions of manipulativeness and other factors to relationship quality.
  • The results show any type of relationship can be marred by manipulativeness but there are ways to escape.

Being in the grips of a manipulative partner can make you feel not only suffocated but powerless. Meg is constantly doing things for her partner that he could easily do himself. Not only does she do the majority of household chores, but he somehow manages to make her feel that if she doesn’t run his errands, it proves he doesn’t love her. Meg is a kind person and she often does favors for her friends, but her partner’s constant demands are starting to get to her. Is there a way she can maintain their relationship as well as her autonomy?

The Personality Traits That Underlie Manipulativeness

According to University of Connecticut’s Meredith Turner (2026), “Manipulativeness is a common, yet complex, feature of interpersonal relationships,” associated with the personality trait of psychopathy along with the tendency to lie and emotionally abuse others. As bad as all of this sounds, there is a surprising lack of research on how these qualities affect how relationships characterized by a manipulative partner manage to survive (or not). The purpose of her research was to examine this research systematically to get some answers.

Turner notes that part of this gap in the literature comes from the “litany of different scales” that assess the quality of a relationship. There are also distinctions that need to be made between the personality traits themselves that contribute to manipulativeness vs. the behaviors that represent such factors as power differentials and the needs of the individual partners.

Meg’s problem seems to lie in the fear that her partner will abandon her if she doesn’t comply with his wishes. Not only does she feel dependent on him (perhaps reflecting her own needs), but he seems to hold some type of power over her that prevents her from standing up for herself. Whatever is causing this, she’s starting to feel that if things don’t change, she’ll need to get out somehow.

Measuring the Relational Costs of Manipulativeness

Beginning with a set of nearly 6,500 journal articles, Turner eventually narrowed the appropriate ones down to 16 after all the inclusion criteria were taken into account. Though small in number, these studies reflected 53 statistical effect estimators and nearly 11,000 participants.

The findings support the author’s initial suspicion that relationships suffer when there is a manipulative partner involved. The key personality trait of Machiavellianism indeed emerged as a significant predictor of poor relationship quality, as did emotional manipulation (e.g., “How often have you tried to make another person feel uneasy?”). There were no effects in the prediction equation of age, gender composition, and type of relationship, suggesting that Machiavellianism's “relational costs are consistent.”

Putting these findings into a larger theoretical context, the UConn psychologist cites “relational maintenance theory,” which contrasts the loving and caring behaviors that keep relationships healthy from the “antisocial behaviors” that tend to erode it. In the short term, manipulative partners do get their way, but over time, their efforts to elicit compliance will be outweighed by detracting from the partner’s feelings of trust and intimacy.

The issue for Meg therefore becomes one of asking whether her increasing discomfort with her partner is due to a general tendency he has to control others or whether it’s something specific to their relationship itself. Turner’s research suggests that it doesn’t really matter what’s causing the partner’s constant efforts to keep Meg in line, just the fact that it happens.

There’s an even larger perspective into which these findings can be placed, furthermore. According to “equity theory,” people will want to leave a relationship in which they feel they’re putting in more than their partner. A manipulative partner leaves the other one “underbenefited.”

How to Get Out of a Manipulative Relationship

In time, all relationships marked by manipulativeness are doomed to fail. The issue is how to minimize the damage when you’re at the receiving end of a manipulative partner. One of the surprising findings of the Turner study was the lack of impact of age, gender, or even closeness of relationship. You can get locked into one of these poisonous relationships with almost anyone. It could be a friend, a neighbor, or even a hairstylist. Knowing you can get out can get you to step one of actually getting out.

It won’t take a complete personality inventory to get you to the next step. How often do you notice your partner playing the shame game with you? Equity theory can help you with this part of the process. Meg’s partner makes her feel that if she doesn’t do all these things for him, it means she’s selfish. Yet, if she’s honest with herself, she knows that she is giving more than she is getting. You don’t have to keep a complete tally of who’s doing what for whom, but overall you should be able to have some ballpark percentage estimate.

Moving on from here, the next step is to analyze the costs of leaving this manipulative partner. How hard will it be to extricate yourself from this destructive relationship? If it’s simply impossible (e.g. due to practical constraints or the joint responsibility of children), then it’s time to have a direct conversation about the inequities in your relationship.

A big question in this last step of the process is whether you still hold feelings for this person. If the erosion has gotten too extreme, you probably don’t. But if there are still emotional connections, be sure to emphasize these while also trying to assert your independence.

To sum up, a manipulative person in a relationship can create strain that can eventually lead to its ending. Knowing when and how to assert your own needs can help that relationship go from inequitable to fulfilling.

item.title: Giftedness Isn’t a Lie. It’s Just Much Broader Than We Realize
item.description:
Intelligence

Giftedness Isn’t a Lie. It’s Just Much Broader Than We Realize

Personal Perspective: We need to change how we define and test for giftedness.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Giftedness is real. You can argue that we find the wrong kids, not that the ruler measures nothing.
  • Signs of giftedness often show up in infancy, yet scores keep moving—real signal, but no single early verdict
  • The fix isn't abolishing gifted ed, but universal screening and widening what we count, like creativity.
Source: Klaus Vedfelt / Getty

When I was a kid, I was placed in special education. Recurrent ear infections had left me with a central auditory processing disorder, and the school’s verdict was that I needed to be sorted into the room for slow learners. I stayed there for years. I was the opposite of the gifted child.

So you can imagine how I felt reading a New York magazine essay by Katie Arnold-Ratliff arguing that “giftedness itself is a lie.” But what you imagine is probably wrong. Instead of ending up as a warrior against gifted education, I’ve become a fierce advocate. Here’s why.

I’ve spent my adult life studying the question What is intelligence, really? I studied cognitive science, earned a Ph.D. at Yale, and wrote a book called Ungifted: Intelligence Redefined, all driven by a desire to redefine intelligence. So I came in sympathetic to her critique. The trouble is that the part she’s right about and the part she’s wrong about are two distinct claims, and the entire article hinges on our not noticing the difference.

Problems With Current Gifted Identification Methods

First, what she gets right. Testing a 4-year-old once and stamping “gifted” on them for life is bad science: A child’s scores keep moving as they develop. What’s more, the equity numbers are a disgrace: About 60 percent of kids in gifted programs are white in a system that’s roughly 40 percent white, and of the 781 students admitted to Stuyvesant last year, eight were Black.

But watch what she says next: She goes from the way we identify gifted kids is broken to giftedness is a lie, and those are wildly different sentences. The first is about a measurement. The second is about reality. The lie isn’t giftedness. The lie is the essentialist label: the fantasy that a Tuesday-morning test reveals a fixed kind of person, a caste you’re assigned at 5 and can never leave, or (in my case) a caste of ungifted that you can never escape.

She doesn’t acknowledge that cognitive ability is one of the most reliably measured and predictively valid constructs in psychology. The longest-running study of intellectually precocious kids, the Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth, has tracked its participants for nearly half a century and finds that ability spotted in childhood predicts patents, doctorates, and creative work decades later, far above base rates. And the claim that enrichment doesn’t help runs straight into one of the most lopsided literatures in all of education: The evidence that well-designed acceleration works is about as settled as anything we have. You can argue that we find the wrong kids. You cannot argue that the ruler measures nothing.

article continues after advertisement

But here’s some interesting nuance. It’s possible to detect at least some signs of giftedness in infancy. Brief tests of infant attention (basically, how fast a baby gets bored with a picture it’s already seen) predict adult IQ and academic achievement years later, independent of how educated the parents are. Of course, those same scores are nowhere near fixed. Follow the same kids over time, and you’ll watch IQ swing around quite a bit, especially in childhood and adolescence.

Is Giftedness Real or a Mirage?

So which is it, real or a mirage? Both, and neither, which is precisely the nuance the article never reaches for. The early signal is real, and a single early score is still no verdict. You have to hold both of those at once.

The fix: Stop betting a child’s future on one test at age 4. It’s exactly why I’ve argued for re-screening kids and assessing them over time.

But the biggest contradiction in the piece is quieter. Arnold-Ratliff writes that a gifted child is just one who performs differently from peers, “rather than any inherent characteristic,” as if the category were drawn in sand. And then, a few paragraphs later, her own reporting blows that up. She notes that highly intelligent kids are far more likely to be diagnosed with autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and she quotes a neuropsychologist describing their “overexcitability,” brains “firing nonstop.” One of her sources says she doesn’t think there are “truly gifted neurotypical children.” Friends, that is not the description of a mirage: That is the description of a real, embodied, neurologically distinct way of moving through the world! It is, in fact, the twice-exceptional and asynchronous development I’ve spent years studying, and that I lived.

So what do we do? We look harder, and we look wider.

First, the fix for a biased front door is not to brick up the building. It’s universal screening: Test every child instead of waiting for an adult to notice them. When districts have done this, they’ve found the low-income, Black, and Hispanic gifted kids who were sitting in the same classrooms the whole time, invisible to a system that was never pointed at them. The cleanest demonstration is Card and Giuliano’s research. (Years ago, I surveyed how states define and identify giftedness, and the variation is staggering, which tells you most of this is a policy choice, not a law of nature.)

Second, widen what counts. The U.S. government’s 1972 definition of giftedness named six dimensions, including creative thinking, leadership, and ability in the visual and performing arts. The creativity researcher E. Paul Torrance estimated that identifying gifted kids by IQ and achievement alone misses about 70 percent of the most creative children, partly because creative kids tend to be unconventional and teachers reliably nominate the pleasers instead. And unlike IQ tests, creativity measures show almost no ethnic gap.

article continues after advertisement

Also, and this bears emphasis: Giftedness is a trait, not a trophy. A gifted child who never becomes eminent was not a mirage. They were a gifted child. We see the gift, we feed it, and we don’t need it to ripen into fame to call it real.

In fact, I would argue that the most revealing moment is Arnold-Ratliff’s own moment. She adored her gifted years, and she also lets slip that she may never have qualified for the program. Read that again. The education that changed her life was never causally connected to the test that supposedly justified it. The problem was never the enrichment. It was the gate. So tear down the gate, not the education. Give every child the enrichment they need, when they need it.

Which brings me back to where I started. The article spends thousands of words on what the gifted label does to the kids who carry it. It never once asks what the other label does, the one I wore, the quiet verdict handed to the kids left behind who are viewed as the slow ones. In ninth grade, a special education teacher pulled me aside and asked, in effect, why I was still in her class. It had never occurred to me that I had a choice. That question moved my ceiling more than any test ever did. So when smart people decide the compassionate move is to throw out the entire idea of human potential, I get twitchy, because the kids who pay for that are never the ones at the citywide gifted school. They’re the ones nobody bothered to look at.

So, is everyone gifted? Probably not. But far more kids are gifted than the gate ever lets in. In Ungifted, I define intelligence as “the dynamic interplay of engagement and abilities in pursuit of personal goals.” It’s incredible what people are capable of when their talents and passions work synergistically and are given the resources to run. Giftedness should be a trajectory you’re allowed to be on, if someone bothers to put you on it. Somebody finally bothered with me. I want to pay this forward.

The gifted child isn’t a mirage. What’s a mirage is the velvet rope we strung around an education that should have belonged to every single student who would benefit from the enriched resources. Take down the rope, widen the lens, screen every kid, and you’ll be astonished by how much potential was sitting in the room the entire time.

item.title: AI is Creating a New Kind of Voyeur
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI is Creating a New Kind of Voyeur

Meet the self-voyeur, someone who watches thought happen and calls it thinking.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • AI produces ideas that feel like yours because it's calibrated to you.
  • The digital self-voyeur mistakes the reward of thinking for the act of it.
  • The danger is that we are all vulnerable and that the difference is almost impossible to feel.
Source: Image by Photorama from Pixabay.

I've been watching something happen to people I know and even respect. And it's taken me a while to understand what I'm actually seeing, but I think I'm on to something.

The other day, a friend of mine posted a new blog entry. It was smart, well-structured and the kind of thing that makes you think and challenges your ideas. So I left a comment and pushed the idea one step further. His response surprised me. It didn't align with the post and there was nothing behind it. Not wrong, just empty in a way I recognized almost immediately. It felt disconnected from the thinking that appeared to have produced the original blog post. My suspicion is that the post had arrived fully cooked—the path from A to B had avoided the bumps of human cognition—arriving finished by way of a large language model. And he seemed genuinely proud of it.

That pride is what's really bothering me. He wasn't pretending, he seems to be genuinely satisfied. The ideas reflected his sensibility and brilliance and it all arrived with his characteristic confidence. And in this case, perhaps even an implicit overconfidence. So he claimed it. And why wouldn't he?

I'm calling this the self-voyeur. Someone who watches thought happen and feels the satisfaction of having thought. It's not a fraud exactly, but something stranger than that.

And it's not laziness. Laziness at least knows what it's avoiding. This is a dissociation between the cognitive event and the feeling it once required. The cognitive friction has been removed from the process. What remains is the reward. And I guess it's fair to call it real. It's just detached from the process that was supposed to produce it.

The mirror is the problem. It's so precisely calibrated to your own sensibility that the reflection feels earned. The ideas come back in your image. Of course you recognize them. Of course they feel like yours. The claim of authorship follows instinctively and feels completely reasonable.

But real thinking leaves an impression and it changes how you see the next problem. AI can generate that output, but it can't generate that change. And the self-voyeur, receiving the output with genuine satisfaction, may never notice what didn't happen.

If you knew you were watching, you'd be a critic. The self-voyeur thinks he's the author. And this perspective is at the heart of this concept. A critic can course-correct, but an author who never wrote anything has no idea there's anything to fix.

The danger isn't "those people over there." The danger is that the technology can tempt any of us into mistaking the experience of thinking for thinking itself.

I find this frightening. Not in some abstract, dystopian way. Frightening because it's already happening to people I know and respect. People who have found a new kind of intellectual pleasure that asks nothing of them, and can't feel the difference.

item.title: Informational Fast Food and the Lost Art of Nuance
item.description:
Media

Informational Fast Food and the Lost Art of Nuance

Steps toward a healthier information diet.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Nuance, empathy, and curiosity are essential for a healthy information diet.
  • Social media algorithms often reward outrage and deepen ideological echo chambers.
  • Socratic questioning helps us challenge assumptions and think more critically.

We often think carefully about what we put into our bodies, yet we rarely apply the same scrutiny to what we put into our minds. As a researcher with a particular interest in online consumer cultures, I often reflect on the effects that spending a sizeable portion of our lives in digital environments can have on us. Just as a diet built entirely on fast food can undermine our physical health, a steady stream of sensationalist headlines and algorithmically curated echo chambers can distort our understanding of the world. So how can we become conscious consumers of information rather than passive recipients of whatever appears in our feeds?

In an era when every topic seems to divide us, the art of nuanced thinking, or the ability to see the complexities in any issue, feels almost forgotten. Social and political issues are increasingly presented to us as binary, implying that "you are either with or against us, right or wrong, ally or enemy". While making it easier for us to feel social belonging once we pick a side, this polarization that initially feels very comfortable and reassuring eventually stifles our ability to engage critically with ideas and to genuinely understand others. In thinking about how we could potentially find a way out of this trap, I remembered the Socratic questioning method that was taught to us at the university many years ago, when I was still a young and bright-eyed psychology student.

The Decline of Nuance

Nuanced thinking is essential for a well-rounded, reflective society. It allows us to appreciate the complexity of issues and see perspectives beyond our own, which is what sets human beings apart from other species. Yet, over the past few decades, the rise of sensationalism fed by social media algorithms that thrive on user engagement has created an environment that rewards emotional and divisive content over thoughtful discourse. Recent research in marketing argues that the media market itself is built around incentivizing virality, opening doors to the proliferation of controversial and adversarial content. While researchers do not always agree about how strongly social media contributes to societal polarization, there is an agreement that we should do more about finding ways to reduce this polarization, or at least avoid making it worse.

The Echo Chambers

The concept of echo chambers is frequently invoked to describe the situation when people are only exposed to one-sided narratives, becoming more certain of their beliefs, even if those beliefs are poorly founded. We have all been there, clicking further and further on those reels and videos recommended to us by algorithms that are presenting us with more and more convincing and interesting but also at times more extreme visions of the topic that we are interested in. As Diaz Ruiz and Nilsson note in their recent study, polarizing content in social media weaponizes truths, half-truths, and value-laden judgments alongside blatant disinformation. They argue that these claims are linked to the deep-seated sense of who we are and where we belong.

Escaping Informational Fast Food

To break free from rigid mental frameworks, we can turn to Socratic questioning. Although this technique is as old as philosophy itself, it is still widely used in psychotherapy and education. It involves asking probing questions that encourage people to examine their beliefs and consider alternative perspectives. Examples include questions that seek clarification (“What exactly is this claim trying to say?”), questions that ask for reasons and evidence (“What evidence supports this claim?”), and questions that probe underlying assumptions (“What assumptions does this argument rely on?”). An additional useful question examines interests and motivations: “Who benefits if people believe this claim?” The goal is to uncover the assumptions and values that shape our beliefs while letting go of the need to always be right. We can also make a habit of reading sources that challenge our beliefs, following media from across the spectrum and engaging respectfully with people who hold different opinions. Doing so will slowly but steadily help us build empathy and understanding, the essential ingredients of nuanced thinking that make us so deeply and profoundly human.

It may not be the easiest thing to do, but these steps away from informational fast food can help us develop intellectual humility and approach our views with openness and curiosity, reminding ourselves that we may not know everything, and that perhaps we need to listen and learn more. I was recently at a conference presenting our research on how algorithms shape online dating. As I was finalizing my presentation, I found myself returning to a quote from Pope Leo XVI's recent encyclical letter, Magnifica Humanitas: “When human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.” In many ways, the challenge of resisting polarization and practicing nuance is part of that duty. The journey toward nuance and empathy may not be easy, but it is essential if we hope to build the balanced, open, and informed society we so urgently need.

item.title: We Built the Casino, Then Blamed the Gambler
item.description:
Compulsive Behaviors

We Built the Casino, Then Blamed the Gambler

Personal Perspective: Sports media profits from gambling but condemns the athletes who gamble.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Sports networks condemn Brendan Sorsby for gambling while airing betting lines paid for by sportsbooks.
  • Gambling is now mainstream, with dedicated betting shows and player props running across daily coverage.
  • Young athletes now see their own over/unders and props, then face punishment for the temptation we created.
  • The networks that could name this hypocrisy stay silent because sportsbooks fund them.
Source: Mart Production / Pexels

Brendan Sorsby is headed for the NFL supplemental draft. The Texas Tech quarterback plans to apply just a week after a Texas judge handed him a temporary injunction on June 8 that briefly reopened his path to the Red Raiders' 2026 season. Within days, the backlash from coaches, conferences, and athletic directors grew loud enough that he withdrew his lawsuit and left college football entirely. He had been ruled ineligible by the NCAA, which found that he had placed roughly $90,000 in wagers across four years, including 40 bets on Indiana football during his freshman season with the Hoosiers. He had also gone through inpatient treatment for gambling addiction.

Debating Recovery and Criticism in Sports Gambling Cases

I wrote about Sorsby once before and argued that the field could offer the structure, routine, and accountability recovery needs. I still believe that. Today I want to talk about the people pointing fingers, because the loudest voices condemning him broadcast from studios paid for by the companies that sell the exact behavior he is being punished for.

The condemnation has been wrapped in the language of sanctity and integrity, and it has echoed everywhere. ESPN columnists wrote that protecting the integrity of competition is job one for any legitimate sports organization, while Fox outlets declared that integrity had left the building. TCU coach Sonny Dykes called the ruling a bad day for college football, then said the quiet part out loud. He admitted he worries his own players might now think it is fine to bet on football, since all they will see in the headlines is that Sorsby bet and now he gets to keep playing. He is right to worry, and the headlines are the smallest part of why.

Consider where these integrity sermons air. In December 2025, ESPN named DraftKings its official sportsbook and odds provider, with DraftKings products woven throughout ESPN's platforms, including its sportsbook, daily fantasy, Pick6, and a betting tab inside the ESPN app. Player props now run daily on SportsCenter, and sportsbook-sponsored segments fill the halftime sets. A network can preach the sanctity of the game in one segment and push the parlay of the day in the next, and almost no one blinks.

article continues after advertisement

Professional Leagues and Their Gambling Ties

The league Sorsby hopes to reach is no cleaner. The NFL prohibits its players from gambling while holding rich partnership deals with FanDuel, DraftKings, and Caesars Entertainment, its official casino sponsor. Among the professionals, no one even bothers to pretend the games and the wagers are kept apart.

When Pete Rose was banned in 1989, gambling was the cardinal sin of American sports, and the wall between the game and the wager felt absolute. That world is gone. In 2026, the wager is the product, woven so tightly into broadcasts that odds, over/unders, and props have become the main attraction.

Athletes have always watched sports media, because they want to know what is being said about them. The young player who once tuned in to learn whether he was respected now learns his personal over/under, his passing prop, and the live line on his next game. We built a machine that whispers a number attached to his own body, on a loop, through the voices he trusts most. Then we act shocked when he reaches for his phone.

This is basic behavioral psychology. You cannot saturate an environment with a stimulus, attach money and status to it, deliver it through the most credible people in the room, and expect the youngest viewers to stay immune. Exposure shapes behavior. Repetition normalizes. Every public health campaign on smoking and junk food rests on that truth. Sports betting is the product we market hardest while punishing hardest the people who consume it.

The institutions best positioned to expose this hypocrisy are funded by the sportsbooks, and a network will not bite the hand that signs its checks. The obvious observation, the one any honest viewer makes within thirty seconds, never makes the broadcast. The silence is a business decision.

The Overlooked Mental Health Toll of Gambling in Sports

article continues after advertisement

There is also a mental health cost we keep ignoring. Sorsby's behavior was framed as addiction, and he sought treatment for it. Gambling addiction is real, it is rising among young adults, teenagers, and even preteens, and it does not appear from nowhere. It is cultivated. We engineered a frictionless, around-the-clock casino that lives in every pocket, then expressed horror when a young man proved susceptible to it.

Betting on your own games is a genuine integrity problem, and I am not waving that away. The selective outrage is its own kind of rot, with institutions that cash gambling checks performing shock at an athlete who did what their advertisers spend billions encouraging millions of strangers to do every night.

Sorsby may become one of the more highly touted names to enter a supplemental draft in years, possibly the first player selected in one since 2019, perhaps welcomed by a league with its own casino sponsor. The irony writes itself. We will keep selling the bet, keep punishing the bettor, and keep wondering why the next young athlete cannot resist a temptation we manufactured, monetized, and beamed straight into his living room. If we want the sanctity of the game back, we can start by being honest about who profits from its erosion. Until then, the outrage is theater, and the house is still collecting.

item.title: How to Pace Yourself in Overloaded Moments
item.description:
Mindfulness

How to Pace Yourself in Overloaded Moments

Practicing nimble, "hovering" mindfulness can help you navigate difficult days.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • To pace yourself through the day, try a nimble mindfulness practice called modulation.
  • Studies show that modulation, a form of paced breathing, helps to relax your central nervous system.
  • Modulation may give you more precise control over your anxiety levels than taking sedative drugs.
Source: Dulcey Lima/ Unsplash.com

To the extent our culture considers pacing, it often gets framed as an all-or-nothing pursuit. At school, at work, and online, we're confronted with “give 110%” messaging that glorifies hustle — and if we reject that or want to dial back, we’re fed equally extreme advice to “quiet quit” or take pricey yoga retreats.

Neither hustle nor sustained withdrawal, however, is all that workable or fulfilling in the long run. That's why, while writing my book The Art of Pacing, I thought a lot about how to navigate the middle of the pacing spectrum, that under-heralded zone that’s more conducive to thriving than the extreme ends.

One reliable way into that zone is mindfulness, but not necessarily the expensive, long-weekend-retreat kind. At times, skillful pacing calls for a nimbler kind of focus, like that of a hummingbird hovering for a few moments before swooping to the next perch.

If you can swing them, extended retreats are a great way to pace yourself. But on a day-to-day basis, the architecture of my life isn’t all that compatible with absolute or prolonged withdrawal. I work with a rotating stable of clients and have two school-age kids. I live what Hindu practitioners call “the life of the householder,” with all the chaos, drudgery, and interruptions that implies.

All of this meant I was eager to meet the psychiatrist and researcher Joseph Arpaia. Arpaia has practiced Buddhist meditation for decades, but he’s also a skilled practitioner of the hummingbird kind of mindfulness. And despite his meditation expertise, he somehow helped me not to feel so bad about being a subpar meditator.

Once Arpaia understood that I was looking for the frozen-juice concentrate version of mindfulness, he taught me how to make the most of my own suspended-hummingbird moments. He demonstrated a practice I now call modulation, which involves breathing at an individualized pace that research shows calms your central nervous system. (Most people's "resonance breathing," or modulation pace, is between 4 and 6 breaths per minute; you can find your own ideal pace by experimenting with paced breathing videos in that range to see what speed feels most comfortable.)

A range of studies attest to modulation’s calming powers. In a 2025 study of people with anxiety, those who practiced this kind of paced breathing had higher heart rate variability than members of a control group, showing that their nervous systems were becoming more relaxed. Other research points to the biology behind these effects. People doing modulation in a 2026 Rutgers brain study had more connections between brain areas governing nervous system control and emotion regulation, hinting that they were actively tamping down their arousal levels.

When I was at Arpaia's office, he had me breathe at my ideal modulation pace for about five minutes while I wore a finger-clip heart rate monitor. Afterward, he studied my heartbeat tracings on his display screen — and pointed out that my brief modulation stint had changed my heart rate pattern more drastically than an IV tranquilizer drug!

That moment felt like a breakthrough. As someone who's tightly wound by nature, I’ve tried my share of anxiety meds that leave me too groggy to function. With modulation, I had more direct control: I could spin down my nervous system to just the degree I wanted, based on how many minutes I continued paced breathing.

Though I now practice modulation nearly every day, I can't say I’ve completely mastered it. Where I run into trouble is that I find the practice hardest to initiate when I need it most. When I’m feeling especially spun-up about a rejection, a personal drama, or a devastating global event, it becomes harder to believe that something as simple as modulation will make a difference.

But when I persist, making a hummingbird-scale leap of faith, the spin-down starts to happen, usually within just a few minutes. And when it does, I’m better able to make big-picture decisions that help me keep a sustainable pace in the long run.

Copyright Elizabeth Svoboda. A version of this article also appeared in my newsletter The Art of Pacing.

item.title: What if Your Success Is a Response to Childhood Pain?
item.description:
Child Development

What if Your Success Is a Response to Childhood Pain?

Personal Perspective: Criticism in childhood can become part of a child's identity.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Children who experience chronic criticism may lose confidence in their abilities.
  • Some high achievers pursue accomplishments to prove their worth and disprove childhood labels.
  • Professional achievement does not automatically erase negative beliefs formed early in life.
klimkin-flower
Source: Pixaboy/svklimkin

One day, my mom took me to my daycare.

There was one red dress that I hated the most, which was my mom’s favorite. I hated it because it was very tight, and it made my belly look even bigger. I was kind of thick, and the dress made it very obvious. So, my mom decided to put me in that red dress.

There was a boy at my daycare who wanted to play. He approached me and started counting my belly rolls. One, two, three… touching each roll with his finger.

I was so shocked and embarrassed that I ran to the other room and hid under the teacher’s table. I did not want to come out. I never wore that dress again.

Looking back, the dress was cute, and my belly rolls were impossible to ignore....

At the time, I didn’t understand why it affected me so much. If this had been an isolated event, maybe I would have laughed it off and forgotten about it, but by then, I had already heard comments about my weight that I was starting to believe.

My stepfather used to call me fat cow, slow, and other things on the way to my daycare, so I thought I was too big, too slow, too bad etc...

When you hear the same thing from an adult over and over, it starts feeling like this is who you are.

As a child, you see them as grown-ups who know what they are doing, who always do the right thing, and who become the example you are expected to follow without question. Children don't have enough experience to question adults. If an adult says something is wrong with you, you assume it must be true.

When criticism is repeated by a parent or caregiver, it can become part of a child's identity (Cooley, 2005). Over time, these messages stop being just comments and start becoming the “truth” a child uses to understand themselves.

So when that boy counted my belly rolls, it was proof that all the things I had been hearing about myself were true. When I hid under the table, I thought there was really something wrong with me.

Another Story

When I went to first grade at 6, a major accident happened to my leg, and I missed half of first grade, joining the class when they had already learned how to do math.

I knew nothing.

On top of that, my elementary school teacher was not supportive. Since I had missed so much school, I did not know the basics, and she did not have much patience, I guess. Plus, everything was in Kazakh, but my native language was Russian. I was raised speaking Russian. My daycare was in Russian, not Kazakh.

So, my teacher would just call me stupid, and everyone would laugh.

The problem was that I was trying to catch up after missing months of school, while also learning in a language that was not spoken at home. At 6 years old, I could not understand the difference. I thought I was struggling because I was stupid. So I guess I lost interest in studying altogether.

Looking back now, I do not think I lost interest in learning. I lost confidence in my ability to learn. Children are naturally curious. But when every mistake is met with criticism, eventually it is safer not to try at all.

I didn’t do homework, didn’t do my best, just put school aside, and enjoyed my life with my stepbrothers' friends, playing on the garages, walking on the pipes, and building tents. It was easier to be the kid who didn't care about school than the kid who tried and failed.

Finding Success But Struggling With Self-Worth

Thank God, later, my mom transferred me to a Russian school, where I thrived, participated in school and local competitions, wrote poems, and shared stories from classic literature. For the first time, I felt capable. But even then, I didn’t feel smart. It was as if that belief existed deeper than any achievement.

I kept getting scholarships, graduated with honors in dentistry, received another scholarship to study abroad, earned my master's degree, and eventually finished my Ph.D. On the outside, my life kept moving forward. On the inside, I was still catching up to the version of myself others seemed to see. I could understand how others saw me, but I struggled to see myself that way. It was as if success didn’t change my identity or who I believed I was.

Looking back, I think I was never “stupid.” I was a child who was misunderstood and unsupported.

And yet, that belief did not disappear just because my results changed. Although I was successful in school and at university, all my life, I was shy and humble, hiding the things I knew and the things I was good at.

Why?

Because I had great teachers: My stepfather would humble me quickly (he would say “All you can do is to destroy”), and so would my elementary school teacher.

I thought being humble meant staying small, staying quiet, and never owning anything I achieved. Even now, if I do something good, it is never good enough.

Maybe you recognize this feeling, too, when something good happens, but instead of feeling proud, your mind moves to what could have been better.

I remember a moment when a professor praised me in front of others. I wanted to disappear. It felt uncomfortable.

I never thought it was a big deal to be an honor student, receive a scholarship, be a single mom, and finish a Ph.D., until other people started to recognize it. Somehow, I needed external confirmation to allow myself to see my own achievements as real. All my life, I felt like I was proving to someone that I was worth something.

It was never really about success. It was about trying to undo an old belief that was in me.

Even when I achieve something, I don’t feel it. I don’t feel satisfaction. Psychologists describe this as overcompensation or achievement-based self-worth. When a child grows up feeling inadequate, they may spend adulthood collecting evidence to prove their value through grades, scholarships, degrees, work, or success. The achievement becomes less about growth and more about disproving the negative beliefs formed in childhood (Crocker & Wolfe, 2001; Flett & Hewitt, 2002).

If you find yourself always racing, rushing, chasing the next achievement, the next degree, the next promotion, or the next goal, ask yourself:

Am I trying to convince someone that I am worthy?

I don’t always have the answer to that question. Sometimes I still catch myself running without stopping to ask why.

My family would always tell me to take a break, acknowledge myself, and recognize that what I had accomplished was a big deal. But sometimes I feel like there is an invisible wall between me and those words.

People say kind things about me, but the words do not make it through. It is as if they hit the wall and bounce back. I hear and understand the words, but somehow I do not absorb them.

The moment someone praises me, I feel like I am shrinking. Part of me wants to change the subject, disappear, or stop listening altogether. I know what they are saying. I just don't believe it yet.

Sometimes I wonder how different my life would have been if nobody had called me stupid, slow, or not good enough. Then I realize that it is better to ask not what happened back then, but what I choose to believe now....

What labels are you still carrying that no longer belong to you?

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Being Right
item.description:
Cognition

The Hidden Cost of Being Right

Do you want the truth or vindication?

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • The desire for certainty often motivates people to prioritize being right over knowing the truth.
  • Intelligence is no protection against such motivated reasoning.
  • Linking beliefs to one's identity makes changing one's mind feel like a personal threat.
  • Intellectual humility is based on the assumption that one's knowledge is always incomplete.

Most people believe they want the truth. I'm not so sure. I think what many of us really want is to be right.

The distinction may seem subtle, but it has enormous consequences for our relationships, our learning, and our mental health.

Being right feels good. It provides certainty in an uncertain world. It reassures us that our beliefs, decisions, and actions make sense. It protects our self-image and gives us confidence. In fact, being right can be psychologically rewarding in much the same way as other pleasurable experiences. We experience a sense of validation, competence, and sometimes even superiority.

The trouble begins when being right becomes more important than discovering what is true.

The Brain's Need for Certainty

Human beings evolved in an environment in which uncertainty could be dangerous. If our ancestors heard a rustling sound in nearby bushes, they often had to make a quick decision. Was it the wind or a predator? Excessive uncertainty could be costly.

As a result, the human brain developed a preference for certainty. We naturally seek patterns, explanations, and conclusions. We want the world to make sense.

Psychologists have long understood that people are uncomfortable with ambiguity. Studies show that uncertainty can increase anxiety and stress. Certainty, even when misplaced, often provides emotional relief.

This helps explain why people frequently cling to beliefs long after evidence suggests they should reconsider them. The belief itself may matter less than the comfort it provides.

Intelligence Is Not Immunity

Many people assume that intelligence protects us from faulty thinking. Unfortunately, research suggests otherwise.

Highly intelligent individuals are often exceptionally skilled at defending their existing beliefs. Rather than using intelligence to discover truth, they may use it to justify conclusions they have already reached.

Psychologists refer to this tendency as motivated reasoning. Instead of objectively evaluating evidence, we unconsciously search for information that supports our existing views and dismiss information that challenges them.

The smarter we are, the better we may become at constructing convincing arguments in support of our preferred position. In other words, intelligence can sometimes make us better lawyers than scientists.

A scientist asks, "What does the evidence suggest?" A lawyer asks, "How can I defend my case?" When it comes to deeply held beliefs, many of us become lawyers.

The Relationship Cost

The desire to be right can create significant problems in personal relationships.

Think about the last argument you had with a spouse, friend, family member, or colleague. How much of the disagreement was about solving a problem, and how much was about proving a point?

Many conflicts escalate because both parties become focused on winning rather than understanding. The irony is that relationships rarely benefit from victory.

A husband may win an argument and lose intimacy. A friend may prove a point and damage trust. A manager may establish authority and undermine collaboration.

The goal of communication is often assumed to be persuasion. In reality, the goal is frequently connection. Connection requires curiosity. Curiosity requires the willingness to be wrong.

The Learning Cost

The desire to be right also interferes with learning.

Every significant advance in knowledge begins with the recognition that previous assumptions may be incomplete or incorrect.

Scientific progress depends on questioning existing ideas. Personal growth depends on questioning existing beliefs. Yet many people treat being wrong as a threat rather than an opportunity.

When we become overly attached to being right, we stop exploring. We stop asking questions. We stop considering alternatives. We become prisoners of our own certainty. Ironically, the people who learn the most are often those who are most comfortable admitting what they do not know.

The Social Media Effect

Modern technology has amplified the problem. Social media platforms reward confidence far more than nuance. People rarely go viral by saying:

"I might be mistaken."

"More research is needed."

"This is a complex issue with multiple perspectives."

Instead, certainty attracts attention. Confidence attracts followers. Outrage attracts engagement. As a result, many people are encouraged to present opinions as facts and assumptions as certainty. The loudest voices often appear to be the most knowledgeable, even when the evidence suggests otherwise.

This creates an environment in which being right becomes a performance rather than a process of discovery.

The Ego's Favorite Activity

At its core, the need to be right is often connected to ego. Our beliefs become intertwined with our identity. Challenges to our ideas begin to feel like challenges to ourselves. Once this happens, changing our minds becomes emotionally difficult.

We are no longer evaluating information. We are defending who we think we are.

This helps explain why discussions about politics, religion, parenting, health, and other emotionally charged topics can become so intense. The conversation is no longer simply about facts. It is about identity. And identity is something people will fight hard to protect.

The Power of Intellectual Humility

Fortunately, there is an alternative.

Psychologists have increasingly studied what is known as intellectual humility. Intellectual humility does not mean lacking confidence or abandoning convictions. It means recognizing that our knowledge is always incomplete.

It involves accepting the possibility that we may be mistaken. It involves remaining open to new evidence. It involves separating our identity from our opinions.

Research suggests that intellectually humble individuals are more open-minded, less polarized, and better able to learn from others. They tend to have more productive conversations and stronger relationships. Most important, they are often closer to the truth because they are willing to revise their beliefs when necessary.

The Freedom of Being Wrong

One of the most liberating realizations in life is that being wrong is not a personal failure. It is a normal part of being human.

Every meaningful lesson we learn requires the recognition that we previously misunderstood something. Every major scientific breakthrough begins with the discovery that an accepted belief was incomplete. Every personal transformation starts with the realization that our current way of thinking may no longer serve us.

Being wrong is not the opposite of growth. It is often the beginning of growth.

The next time you find yourself in an argument, consider asking a different question. Instead of asking, "How can I prove that I am right?" Ask, "What can I learn here?"

The answer may improve your relationships, expand your understanding, and reduce the stress that comes from constantly defending a position.

Because while being right feels good, learning something new may feel even better.

item.title: Your Brain on a GLP-1: What We Know About the Mental Side
item.description:
Body Image

Your Brain on a GLP-1: What We Know About the Mental Side

Emerging evidence regarding the psychological effects of GLP-1 medicines.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 medicines are known for their medical effects. Few know about their psychosocial effects.
  • For many GLP-1 users, the psychological changes are as powerful as the physical changes.
  • Psychological changes differ across people while falling into eight general categories.

Samantha had enjoyed her weekend cooking ritual for years. Four months into Zepbound (a popular GLP-1 medicine), however, something changed. She stood in her kitchen on a Saturday morning and made the dish she always made. It came out exactly right. But she ate just a quarter of it, put the rest away, and didn't photograph the dish for social media for the first time she could remember. Her cooking ritual suddenly felt empty.

Sam's formerly intrusive food noise was finally gone. She expected to feel liberated. Happier. But what she felt instead was lost, as if she'd accidentally wandered off a well-known trail. Like millions of other people now using GLP-1 medicines, Samantha knew what physical changes to expect from the treatment. But no one prepared her for the psychological changes.

Here is a summary of what recent science tells us about the mental side of the GLP-1 journey.

Source: Thomas Rutledge, PowerPoint

Food Noise

Within weeks of starting a GLP-1 medicine, the constant background preoccupation with food (the mental negotiating, the anticipatory planning, the low-level demand of appetite) can go from relentless to near-absent.1 Many people describe this change as the most immediate psychological effect of the medicine. But the sudden silence can also reveal the stress, emotions, and problems the food noise was masking. For the unprepared GLP-1 user, freedom from food noise may arrive as a mixed blessing requiring new strategies for managing previously concealed thoughts and feelings.

Shame and Stigma

Many GLP-1 users carry a private burden: the belief that needing this medicine is proof of something they failed to do on their own.2 This feeling is the direct result of decades of cultural messaging that classified weight as a character issue rather than a hormonal one. Public or private, however, the shame many users feel about starting GLP-1 treatment is an important emotional barrier. For example, it affects (1) whether people participate in the treatment, (2) how likely they are to tell the people they care about, and (3) whether they allow themselves to keep using something long-term that is working.

Emotional Eating

Emotional eating is a learned coping behavior with an established neurological basis: Food reliably activates the brain's soothing and reward pathways, providing short-term relief. GLP-1 medicines reduce the biological urgency of eating, including emotional eating symptoms for some users.3 They do not, however, address the emotional conditions that food was managing. Many people, several months into GLP-1 treatment, find themselves experiencing symptoms related to depression, anxiety, or stress that they had been eating around for years. For them, there is a need to develop emotion-regulation strategies that food was previously providing.

Identity (Who Am I Becoming?)

The body can change faster than our self-concept. The person who looks different in the mirror still carries the reflexes, habits, and self-perception assembled over years of living in the previous body. They still reach for the wider seat. Still brace for a social reaction that no longer arrives. Psychologists call this identity lag: the gap between what the body has become and how the person inhabiting it still experiences the world. With GLP-1 medicines, this is not a sign that something is wrong.4 It is simply the measured pace of psychological adaptation, which has always been slower than biology.

Body Image

Weight-loss research consistently documents a surprising finding: Losing weight does not automatically improve how you feel about your body. Early in a GLP-1 journey, body image dissatisfaction can actually increase, because the changing body draws more attention to itself, including to aspects the person hadn't focused on before.5 Loose skin, resulting from rapid weight loss, sits at the center of this and is a common source of private emotional struggles for GLP-1 users. For many people, happiness about their breakthrough weight loss arrives mixed with something akin to grief. That grief deserves acknowledgment as a part of the GLP-1 treatment experience. Progress and struggle can co-exist.

Relationships

Research shows that relationship stability tends to decrease following significant weight loss, even when both partners wanted the change.6 Friendships built around shared struggles with food and weight, for example, can destabilize when one person's situation changes. A romantic partner's response to significant weight loss can range from deeply supportive to subtly complicated, through no fault of either person. And the greater the weight loss, the greater the potential for social upheaval. Understanding this is power, not pessimism. The information can empower the person to anticipate and prepare for relational changes instead of being caught off guard.

Mental Health

Mental health and obesity are bidirectionally linked. Depression, anxiety, trauma, and binge eating each predict weight gain over time, while clinical obesity is associated with elevated rates of mood disorders and disordered eating. In clinical trials, GLP-1 medicines generally improve depression and anxiety measures.7 The same GLP-1 journey, however, can lead to new or worsening symptoms for some users. Individual attention to mental health symptoms while using GLP-1 medicines is strongly encouraged.

The Long Game

The clinical evidence is unequivocal: When GLP-1 treatment stops, weight typically returns.8 This is a predictable effect of stopping a medicine intended for a chronic condition. Adopting long-term medication for a chronic weight condition, however, requires emotional acceptance in addition to financial means and intellectual understanding. It is one thing to know that obesity has biological roots. It is a different emotional task to accept that managing it requires indefinite medical treatment.

Summary

Millions of people are now using GLP-1 medicines. Research regarding their medical effects is extensive. Yet the attention to what they do psychologically remains comparatively modest and catches many users by surprise. Understanding both the physical and psychological effects of GLP-1 medicines, however, is the difference between a conventional treatment experience and an opportunity for real transformation.

item.title: The Invisible Relationship Task That's Destroying Desire
item.description:
Relationships

The Invisible Relationship Task That's Destroying Desire

Attraction fades when partnership turns into management

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Strong relationships share both visible tasks and invisible labor.
  • Attraction can suffer when one partner feels responsible for everything.
  • Helping is different from sharing ownership of daily responsibilities.

When couples talk about losing attraction in a long-term relationship, they often focus on communication problems, unresolved conflict, or a lack of quality time. While those factors certainly matter, another issue is showing up with increasing frequency in conversations about intimacy: the mental load.

Many people describe feeling less like a romantic partner and more like the person responsible for keeping life running. They are the one remembering appointments, managing schedules, anticipating problems, and making sure important tasks don't fall through the cracks. Over time, that experience can affect more than stress levels. It can change how partners see one another and, in some cases, how much desire they feel within the relationship.

At first glance, the connection may seem surprising. Household management and romantic attraction appear to occupy different domains. Yet many people describe a gradual shift that occurs when one partner becomes the default organizer, planner, and problem solver. What begins as an imbalance in responsibility can eventually influence feelings of closeness, support, and partnership.

One of the most common sentiments I hear from clients is some version of, "I feel like I'm carrying everything."

They are not necessarily talking about doing more chores. They are talking about carrying the responsibility of remembering, anticipating, and managing. The burden is less about the tasks themselves and more about being the person who must constantly think about them.

The Invisible Work Behind Daily Life

The mental load refers to the cognitive labor involved in managing everyday responsibilities. It includes remembering birthdays, scheduling appointments, planning meals, tracking children's activities, anticipating future needs, and monitoring the countless details that keep a household functioning smoothly.

Unlike visible tasks, this work often happens entirely behind the scenes.

Most people can identify who washed the dishes or folded the laundry. It is far more difficult to see who noticed the refrigerator was empty, remembered that a permission slip was due, or realized that next week's schedule required rearranging childcare plans. Because this labor is largely invisible, it is easy to underestimate.

In many relationships, one partner gradually assumes responsibility for managing these details. The shift is not always intentional. One person may be naturally more organized or quicker to notice when something needs attention. Over time, however, they become the person who remembers, plans, follows up, and keeps track of what still needs to be done.

Eventually, the issue is no longer about who completed a particular task but about who feels responsible, every day, for making sure life stays on track.

How the Mental Load Changes Relationship Dynamics

Attraction does not exist separately from the way partners experience one another.

When one person carries a disproportionate share of the mental load, stress often becomes a constant presence. Even during moments intended for relaxation or connection, part of their attention remains occupied by unfinished responsibilities, looming deadlines, or the next problem that needs solving.

Chronic stress alone can create obstacles to intimacy. When someone feels mentally overloaded, it becomes more difficult to access the emotional and physical availability that close relationships require.

But stress is only part of the story.

Over time, unequal responsibility can also create resentment, which develops through repeated experiences in which one partner feels solely accountable for ensuring that important things get done.

As this pattern continues, the relationship itself can begin to feel different.

The partner carrying the mental load may no longer experience the other person as a fully engaged teammate. Instead, they may feel as though they are supervising, reminding, coordinating, or following up. Many describe feeling more like a manager than a partner.

That distinction matters. Feelings of mutuality, respect, and partnership often support healthy desire. When one person consistently occupies a parental or managerial role, it can become difficult to maintain the sense of equality that romantic attraction often depends upon.

Simply put, it is hard to feel connected to someone when you feel responsible for them.

Helping Versus Sharing Ownership

Conversations about the mental load often become frustrating because partners may have very different definitions of contribution.

A common response from the partner carrying less of the mental load is, "Just tell me what you need me to do." While perhaps well-intentioned, this response can miss an important point: For the person carrying the mental load, the burden often begins long before the task itself. Someone still has to notice the problem, remember it needs attention, create a plan, assign responsibility, and monitor follow-through. In other words, someone is still managing.

This highlights an important distinction between helping and sharing ownership: Helping means completing a task after someone else has identified it. Sharing ownership means taking responsibility for noticing, planning, and following through without relying on another person to direct the process. Both forms of contribution have value. However, they are not experienced in the same way.

When one partner consistently carries responsibility for organizing and overseeing daily life, they may continue to feel alone in the work, even when the other person is willing to help.

Creating a More Balanced Partnership

Addressing the mental load is not about assigning blame or keeping score. Most couples do not arrive at these dynamics intentionally. Instead, responsibilities often evolve gradually until one partner becomes the default manager of family life.

Couples that navigate the mental load successfully tend to move beyond conversations about who is helping whom to develop systems, routines, and expectations that allow both partners to participate in managing the responsibilities of daily life.

When that happens, the relationship begins to feel less like a hierarchy and more like a partnership—and partnership is often one of the conditions that allows intimacy to flourish.

item.title: How Emphasizing Followership Can Combat Leader Narcissism
item.description:
Leadership

How Emphasizing Followership Can Combat Leader Narcissism

Top-level leaders' salaries and perks could contribute to narcissism.

Posted June 16, 2026

Key points
  • Selecting leaders based on personal accomplishments and self-promotion can create more narcissistic leaders.
  • Leader development could fuel narcissism.
  • Leadership development, including the followers, is better.

Recently, in a blog post and publication, we suggested that certain HR practices can fuel leader narcissism in organizations (Mitchell, et al., 2026). Leader-centricism may be to blame because there is a tendency to hire, promote, and develop leaders who are self-centered and self-promoting. Another strategy for combating leader narcissism is to focus on the followers. Here are four ways to do this:

  1. Change the Leader Mindset. There is a pervasive belief that leaders create leadership, but leadership requires a collaboration between leaders and followers. Once we realize this, we can stop viewing leaders as the epicenter of leadership and move beyond an HR focused solely on leaders and leader development. Redefining leadership as composed of both leading and following will limit the primary focus on those at the top and consider more holistic ways of developing leadership.
  2. Change Leader Selection Practices. In leader selection, we ask candidates to focus on their past accomplishments—which may be advantageous to more self-centered, narcissistic individuals who are focused on (and expert at) articulating how their personal efforts have led to success. Instead, candidates should be asked about how they accomplished successful outcomes with others. Giving greater weight to selecting those leaders who have a sense of “we-ness,” rather than being “me-focused.” In hiring and promotion, emphasis should be placed on relationship-building skills, team orientation, and developing and including followers, instead of an individual’s personal accomplishments.
  3. Change Leader Development into Leadership Development. If leadership is created by leaders and followers collaborating, then developing only the leaders is not only an ineffective strategy, but it reinforces the idea that leaders are more important—potentially fueling leader narcissism. Development programs should include followers, and the emphasis should be on relationship-building skills and organizational culture development—areas that promote leaders and followers working together.
  4. Change How Leaders Are Evaluated and Rewarded. Simply looking at how the performance of most leaders is evaluated—with a focus on exerting influence, decision-making, strategic thinking, and leadership “presence”—focuses primarily on the leader, omitting followers in the leadership “equation.” To keep from reinforcing a narcissistic viewpoint, more attention should be given to leaders’ relationship-building efforts, supporting others, and emphasizing shared efforts and responsibilities.

The dramatic discrepancy between top-level leaders/CEOs and rank-and-file employee pay (in many cases exceeding a 200-to-1 ratio) also could encourages narcissism as these financially well-rewarded individuals often see themselves as better, and more important, than followers.

In sum, by putting leaders on a pedestal and selecting, developing, and rewarding leaders, while neglecting the importance of followers and followership in co-creating real leadership in organizations, it is no wonder that there seem to be so many self-centered, narcissistic leaders. The antidote is to recognize the importance of followers in the leadership equation and select and develop leaders who best appreciate that their leadership effectiveness relies on the power and potential of followership.

This post was co-authored by Ron Riggio and Toby Newstead.
